title: Does making a sequel diminish a director's reputation as an artist?

commenti.body: [removed]
Making a shitty sequel to cash in doesn’t help a reputation, but there have been many amazing sequels (Godfather II comes to immediate mind) that only strengthened their director’s legacy.
[removed]
[removed]

I think it’s entirely dependent on context. There are plenty of sequels with clear artistic merit. There are even more that were clearly made for money.

The first have no less artistic merit than a non-sequel and the latter are no better nor any worse than a standalone film made exclusively because the studio believes it will make money.

The only question for any movie IMHO is: Does it work? Being a sequel or not doesn’t factor in.
This is my view as well.

It depends: if the second part is just a cash grab, yes. If it’s a valid argument exploration, no.the Godfather 2 is great, the Godfather 3 is awful.

Batman Begins is meh, The Dark Knight is great. And so on.

Did Ozu make sequels? He remade his own film on more than one occasion. I'm only familiar with his output Late Spring onwards so I'm curious.

Anyway I don't think being a sequel itself has an impact. In fact, if the sequel is bad but the original is great, the sequel will be forgotten with time.

>The question then becomes, is it intrinsically more artistically valuable for a filmmaker to solely make standalone works or does the artistic quality of a sequel supersede any qualms one may have regarding its inception? Do you "respect" a director more for one more than the other?

I don't think there's anything inherently artistically inferior about sequels and the like. You've already adduced filmmakers who dabbled in sequels, prequels and remakes. But the same argument can also be attached to other artists: Is Virgil any lesser a poet for having written essentially a sequel to The Odyssey? Is Parsifal any less a great work of art for being a prequel to Lohengrin?

I think it also partially depends on what KIND of sequel we're talking about: if the filmmaker is trying to tell a story whose scope exceeds one film - Lord of the Rings and The Hobbit are good example, but so is the Soviet War and Peace, David Lean's putative Mutiny on the Bounty and many other such projects. That's obviously has more artistic merit than just making a film and then, off the back of its success, doing a sequel.

Filmmakers who had dabbled in this more traditional kind of sequel were at great pains to present it as if its just another part of a great organic whole: The Godfather sequels are like that, and George Lucas made such (fallacious) remarks about his further forays into Star Wars. Nevertheless, as the examples I've enumerated above show, even those kinds of sequels are nothing to be ashamed of, intrinstically.

There are plenty of great sequels made by the same director as the original film. Dark Knight, of course. Godfather 2. Spiderman 2. Terminator 2. 

It's all about adding new juice to an already great and well-established story. Many do fail because they're trying too hard to recreate the magic of the original, but as they say, you can't catch lightning in a bottle twice.

What bugs me so much about Joker 2 is that they were partway there. Can't have a Joker sequel without the added juice of Harley Quinn – and they had it in the bag. An opportunity to do a twisted love story filled with crime, like Bonnie & Clyde and Natural Born Killers. 

Dark Knight introduced one of the greatest villain performances in, ironically, Heath Ledger's Joker. Godfather brought in the backstory of Vito Corleone. Spiderman 2 brought in one of the most popular bad guys in the Spiderman universe, Doc Ock. Terminator 2 turned Arnie into a good guy and had another Terminator come in to kill John Connor as a kid. All great premises on their own, and freshened up the original story just enough to be good movies.

I think Todd Phillips' ego got in the way and he wanted to make something really cool and different, and he shat the bed with Joker 2.

To the extent that The Good, the Bad and the Ugly is a sequel - yes. I believe that Late Spring is the first of the Noriko trilogy (although I will concede that, much like The Man with No Name, Hara plays variations of the character as opposed to having a narrative through line in the classical sense).

I don’t think so.

A bad original movie would have far greater impact.

One of the problems is a cash grab or a sequel more tied to a directors vision rather than a plausible story could impact reputation.

But a cohesive story routinely boosts a directors profile.
I really don’t think those films are sequels in the way one would usually use that term.
Which is why I stated "to the extent".
You’re conflating two different things.

>is it intrinsically more artistically valuable for a filmmaker to solely make standalone works or does the artistic quality of a sequel supersede any qualms one may have regarding its inception?

The best example I have for this question is Richard Linklater's *Before* trilogy. None of the sequels were cash-ins, they were opportunities to continue to engage with and examine the characters. The audience got to experience the changes in life situation, wisdom, etc. of the two leads. While each film could easily be viewed on their own and stand up well, the impact of all three viewed chronologically is very strong.

>Do you "respect" a director more for one more than the other?

The respect comes more from the quality of the sequel(s), not the fact that they do or don't exist.

My best example--The Indiana Jones franchise. No problems with the first 2 sequels, no respect lost for Spielberg in any meaningful way. *Crystal Skull* felt like a cash-in and one of the worst ideas Spielberg ever allowed to become a reality (I know that Lucas is also very much to blame, but Spielberg's name is on it).

Making a great sequel has the same effect as making a great movie. Conversely, making a bad sequel has the same effect as a bad movie. It being a sequel doesn't have any consequence. 

However, I would say that it affects the first film. As it can be overshadowed by the sequel.

Good examples. In the former, the sequels are both thematically and narratively justified, adding on to the first film as opposed to Indy 4 (I haven't seen 5 but by all accounts the same applies). 

The consensus does seem to be that the said reputation does indeed depend on the "artistic integrity" (for lack of a better term) of the sequels.
The Norikos of Late Spring, Early Summer, and Tokyo Story are three *really* different characters. It makes sense to call these a trilogy, but direct sequel is a bit too far imo.

This was my thinking. 

When you say "overshadowed", do you solely mean in the case wherein the sequel is better? Or would you argue that the effect is additive? For instance, would you say that The Godfather Part II or The Empire Strikes back overshadow their predecessors or add to the overall narrative?

*Dial of Destiny* is literally one of the worst films I've seen in the last few years. I mostly blame the writing and editing. I had respect for James Mangold before that, I hope this doesn't derail his career too badly, and *A Complete Unknown* looks interesting.
I'd only say it overshadows the original if it's bad. If it's good, or better than the original, I'd say it only adds to it.

I take your point but I'm not sure I referred to them as direct sequels? I believe it was Ozu himself who referred to Late Spring / Early Summer / Tokyo Story as a trilogy, thus implying, at least to my understanding, that they were, for lack of a better term, "thematic sequels" (although as you've stated, the three Norikos are distinct from one another). 

The question in itself is interesting, though, as to whether or not a thematic sequel can be considered a sequel (at least semantically). Perhaps I should have excluded Ozu from the list (in the same way I didn't include Leone), though, as you are the second person to have brought this point up.
I guess it comes down to the definition of sequel.

The issue you seem to have is that the Joker sequel wasnt the movie you wanted.
It was the sequel to the first one, and in no way was the Aurther Fleck in that movie capable of becoming the criminal mastermind many wanted him to be.

Just like the crowd outside the courthouse, they too wanted him to be the devil may care criminal mastermind that he clearly is not.

The idea of this post being inspired by The Joker and positioning it as a bastion of high artistic integrity feels disingenuous to me. It’s a film that capitalizes on an already popular character from a massive franchise, designed to appeal to a broader audience. When it comes to artistic ‘integrity,’ it’s already scraping the bottom of the barrel with this manipulative practice. To add to that, The Joker heavily borrows from classic films like Taxi Driver and The King of Comedy, while positioning itself as original. Whether or not it’s an enjoyable movie, it doesn't stand as an example of high artistic achievement.

It’s not the act of making sequels that makes movies worse, as that would imply there’s no story worth telling beyond a single film's 90 minute runtime. The issue lies with how the sequel is handled. For instance, *The Last Jedi* didn’t fail because it was a sequel or because it had a different director than *The Force Awakens*. It failed for a variety of reasons.

Take Rian Johnson’s insistence on including a WWII bomber-style scene. You could argue that this was Johnson staying true to his own artistic vision. However, this came at the expense of the internal logic of the Star Wars universe, which, in my opinion, was damaged beyond repair. Even when directors are pursuing their artistic integrity, that doesn’t necessarily result in a better film, especially when it undermines the world they’re building within. 

The real problem isn't just one thing. Sometimes directors prioritize their own vision over the consistency of the world they're working in, and sometimes the studio forces out a cash-grab sequel and directors have no vision at all. A sequel can absolutely be artistically valid, but only if it respects the story's universe, and has a reason to exist beyond financial gain, which doesn't have to be the exclusive reason for a film's existence, and doesn't diminish the film if it's *part* of its genesis.

>The idea of this post being inspired by The Joker and positioning it as a bastion of high artistic integrity feels disingenuous to me. 

The post was inspired by the negative reception to the sequel and the subsequent reappraisal of Todd Phillips as a director. At no point, other than to mention this very fact, do I call it a "a bastion of high artistic integrity " or even imply that this is how I feel about it, this is purely your interpretation of my post. To be fair, that's not to say I didn't enjoy the first film either, although I'm much more a fan of the films that inspired it, which you've mentioned.  

>It’s a film that capitalizes on an already popular character from a massive franchise, designed to appeal to a broader audience. When it comes to artistic ‘integrity,’ it’s already scraping the bottom of the barrel with this manipulative practice. 

Agree and disagree. It is a re-skin of Scorsese's work, to be sure, but scraping the bottom of the barrel and being manipulative is essentially what most comic books films have been doing for a quarter of a century at this point, relying on a formulaic approach to moviemaking and adjusting their marketing for this very effect. That's not to say these two approaches are mutually exclusive either, but I doubt Joker was really aiming at appealing to the cinephile crowd. You and I may disagree on this point, but I see it more as a gateway film that may help a more casual audience get interested in more artistic films. 

>It’s not the act of making sequels that makes movies worse

This was never my point, or question. Some do, some don't, I was asking how the act of making a sequel impacts a director's reputation. 

>*The Last Jedi* didn’t fail because it was a sequel or because it had a different director than *The Force Awakens*. It failed for a variety of reasons.

As an addedum to my previous point, Rian Johson's reputation suffered as a result of making that film. There are a plethora of reasons why that film is bad, which have been covered extensively. 

>However, this came at the expense of the internal logic of the Star Wars universe, which, in my opinion, was damaged beyond repair. Even when directors are pursuing their artistic integrity, that doesn’t necessarily result in a better film, especially when it undermines the world they’re building within.

This is a good point, and more in line with the question I asked. There have been quite a few examples as of late (Beau is Afraid, Babylon and Megalopolis) where directors have been "true to their vision" and it backfiring on them (whether critically or commercially, or both). Artistically, one may respect them for going all in on their vision (Coppola famously selling part of his vinyard to finance his film, which ended up being a flop) but it also has to be stated that these films did not land in the way they expected, thus negatively affecting their reputation. 

>The real problem isn't just one thing. Sometimes directors prioritize their own vision over the consistency of the world they're working in, and sometimes the studio forces out a cash-grab sequel and directors have no vision at all. 

Very true, and their artistic standing suffers from it. Obviously, the financial imperatives have to be taken into account, but I have to say that I've always respected directors who've turned down money in order to not damage their work or reputation. 

>A sequel can absolutely be artistically valid, but only if it respects the story's universe, and has a reason to exist beyond financial gain, which doesn't have to be the exclusive reason for a film's existence, and doesn't diminish the film if it's *part* of its genesis.

This is a given, but again, not really what I asked. I will concede that it is a multi-faceted question, and there are so many variables to take into account, but the crux of the issue was really to ascertain whether or not there was more artistic merit in creating standalone films (regardless of whether or not a sequel is warranted / succesful) then to make a sequel to one's work or those of others.
